strengths: The paper addresses a relevant provenance problem and usefully distinguishes detection from user attribution, including user-dependent and worst-1% performance metrics.

The experiments report strong clean-image results across three generator datasets, explore populations up to one million users, and examine watermark length, detection thresholds, common corruptions, and selection runtime.
A-BSTA improves watermark separation and lower-tail attribution performance over Random and NRG in the reported experiments. Explicit pseudocode and derivations make the approach inspectable.
weaknesses: Novelty and positioning are insufficiently established. User-specific watermarks, minimum-distance codebooks, and nearest-codeword attribution are closely connected to classical digital fingerprinting and error-correcting codes, which receive inadequate discussion. A-BSTA primarily truncates an existing search algorithm and changes its initialization. Comparisons against structured codebooks such as BCH codes and matched-compute randomized search are needed.

The false-detection guarantee is not established for the proposed method. Section 7.6 applies Theorem 3 although A-BSTA violates its independent-selection assumption. Appendix A.4 also factors match events sharing the same decoded string, which is invalid for fixed codebooks. For example, with uniform two-bit decoding, codebook {00,11}, and threshold 0.75, the actual FDR is 0.5, whereas Equation 11 gives 0.4375.

The binomial analysis relies on independent decoded bits and, for watermarked content, identical per-bit recovery probabilities. These assumptions are not validated for the neural decoders or post-processing conditions. Estimating average bit accuracy and the frequency of ones does not establish independence or the required per-bit bias bounds. Consequently, the empirical applicability of the probabilistic guarantees remains unresolved.

The large-scale and false-positive claims exceed the evidence. The 100-million-user result assumes channel accuracy and codebook distances rather than demonstrating them, and Table 4 supplies a 6% FDR upper bound, which does not establish near-zero false detection. Only 1,000 negative images are evaluated; even zero errors would permit an approximately 0.3% one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. Attribution latency and registration-cost scaling are also not established at the claimed deployment scale.

Robustness evidence is limited to one modified HiDDeN backbone, mostly training-matched corruptions, and one black-box evasion attack. The adversarial experiments have TDR and TAR equal to zero; their low SSIM establishes distortion for that attack, rather than general resistance to limited-query adversaries. Quality-constrained attack success rates and attribution-specific collusion or framing evaluations are missing.

Content preservation and cross-modal generality are insufficiently evaluated. Image SSIM measures post-processing damage without quantifying original-to-watermarked fidelity. The text experiment uses human-written WikiText-2 passages and constrained paraphrasing, with a watermark-loss weight of 10,000 but no semantic-preservation or fluency evaluation. High recovery accuracy therefore does not establish a useful accuracy–quality tradeoff or convincing performance on generated text.
